response.query: Which XAI methods are compatible with our chosen architectures (3D CNN, transformer) and what are estimated compute costs (occlusion complexity, SHAP approximations, LRP applicability) in GPU-hours for full-scale runs?
response.answer: For 3D CNNs, LRP and SHAP are compatible; for transformers, SHAP and attention mechanisms work best. Compute costs vary, but SHAP is generally more resource-intensive than LRP.

results.title: An ensemble of pre-trained transformer models for imbalanced multiclass malware classification - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: An ensemble of pre-trained transformer models for imbalanced multiclass malware classification - ScienceDirect
# An ensemble of pre-trained transformer models for imbalanced multiclass malware classification. API call sequences made by malware are widely utilized features by machine and deep learning models for malware classification as these sequences represent the behavior of malware. Moreover, BERT or CANINE, the pre-trained transformer models, outperforms in classifying highly imbalanced malware families according to evaluation metrics: F1-score and AUC score. > *RQ.5: What is the effect of ensemble of pre-trained transformer models, BERT and CANINE, which is based on bagging for imbalanced multiclass malware classification?*. Again, to the best of our knowledge, a bagging-based ensemble of pre-trained transformer models has been used for the first time in malware classification. In this study, we have leveraged several deep learning models for highly imbalanced multiclass malware classification based on API calls, which are inherently sequence problems. ### Deep learning based sequential model for malware analysis using windows exe API calls. Many research works were focused on static and dynamic analysis-based methods to detect malware (Demirkıran et al., 2022; Nawaz et al., 2022; Maniriho et al., 2024b). This paper presents MeMalDet, a novel memory analysis-based malware detection technique using deep autoencoders and stacked ensemble learning. We introduce an improved dataset with temporal attributes enabling more realistic evaluations of memory-based malware detection techniques under concept drift (temporal data split). MeMalDet combines the benefits of representation learning and supervised machine learning ensemble classification for effective malware detection over time using memory analysis. While traditional signature-based malware detection methods or statistical analysis have proven to be ineffective and time-consuming, recently data-driven *Artificial Intelligence* (AI) techniques, i.e. In this paper, we propose a XAI framework for behavioral malware detection problems and evaluate the usefulness of four XAI methods (SHAP, LIME, LRP and Attention mechanism) on three datasets with different size, sequence length and number of classes, by which we could evaluate the strengths and weaknesses – from effectiveness and efficiency point of views – of recurrent deep architectures (i.e. Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) models), and their applicability in the modern *Cyber Security* (CS) scenarios. * ### Using 3D-VGG-16 and 3D-Resnet-18 deep learning models and FABEMD techniques in the detection of malware.

results.title: xAI Runs the World's Most Powerful Compute Cluster 🤖 - Voronoi
results.content: ##### Where Data Tells the Story. ###### Home. ###### Support. xAI Runs the World's Most Powerful Compute Cluster 🤖 - Voronoi. # xAI Runs the World's Most Powerful Compute Cluster 🤖. * With an estimated 200,000 Nvidia H100 chips, **xAI** has the largest compute cluster globally located in Memphis, TN. * xAI’s compute cluster can hit 20.6 on a log₁₀ scale for non-sparse operations per second, which is over **400 quintillion calculations each second**. * Meanwhile, **Meta, Oracle, and Microsoft/OpenAI** run compute clusters with 100,000 H100 equivalents. ### Supercomputers Are Getting More Powerful and Expensive. Today, xAI's Colossus supercomputer uses an estimated $7 billion in hardware—outpacing Meta's 100K by around $3 billion. Overall, acquisition costs of the most powerful supercomputers grow by twofold every 13 months. Following a similar trend, the power demand for these compute clusters has increased by 1.9 times each year since 2019, with some local grids unable to provide enough power capacity to a single location.
